subject: obstetrics-gynaecology
title: Fetal malpresentations: breech types, external cephalic version and assisted delivery maneuvers

steps.tx: **Breech presentation** occurs when the fetal caudal pole occupies the lower uterine segment, complicating three to four percent of term deliveries. The three primary morphological varieties are frank breech (hips flexed, knees extended; most common at sixty-five to seventy percent), complete breech (both hips and knees flexed), and footling or incomplete breech (one or both feet prolapsed below the buttocks).
steps.say: Breech presentation occurs in three to four percent of term pregnancies. The main types are frank breech with extended legs, complete breech with flexed hips and knees, and footling breech where one or both feet prolapse downward.

rows: Hips flexed, knees fully extended along trunk
Both hips flexed and both knees flexed (cannonball)
One or both feet extend below fetal buttocks

steps.tx: To reduce the requirement for cesarean delivery, **external cephalic version (ECV)** is routinely offered to all women with uncomplicated singleton breech presentation at thirty-six to thirty-seven weeks gestation. Under continuous ultrasound surveillance and uterine tocolysis with beta-mimetics (terbutaline), gentle transabdominal manual pressure rotates the fetus into a cephalic presentation, achieving success rates of approximately fifty percent.
steps.say: External cephalic version is offered at thirty-six to thirty-seven weeks to rotate the fetus into a head-first position. Using ultrasound guidance and tocolysis to relax the uterus, manual pressure achieves successful rotation in about fifty percent of cases.

left.title: Contraindications to ECV
points: Non-reassuring fetal heart rate pattern on CTG
Severe oligohydramnios or rupture of membranes
Uterine malformation or prior classical cesarean

right.title: Procedural safeguards
points: Confirm reactive non-stress test before attempt
Continuous ultrasound visualization of fetal heart rate
Administer Anti-D immunoglobulin to Rh-negative mothers
Immediate emergency cesarean capability on site

steps.tx: Vaginal breech delivery mandates a hands-off approach until spontaneous expulsion of the fetal body to the umbilicus. If fetal arms remain extended above the head, the **Lovset maneuver** is performed. The obstetrician grasps the fetal pelvis with thumbs on the sacrum and rotates the trunk one hundred and eighty degrees, keeping the fetal back anterior to deliver the posterior arm under the pubic symphysis.
steps.say: Vaginal breech birth requires a hands-off approach until the umbilicus delivers spontaneously. For extended arms, the Lovset maneuver rotates the baby one hundred and eighty degrees, keeping the back anterior to deliver the arms beneath the pubic bone.

vis.alt: Multi-panel diagram showing the Lovset maneuver: obstetrician rotates the fetal trunk 180 degrees to deliver extended arms under the pubic symphysis during vaginal breech delivery.
vis.caption: Lovset maneuver for extended arms in vaginal breech delivery

steps.tx: Delivery of the aftercoming fetal head represents the most hazardous stage of breech delivery, as the unyielding maternal pelvis can entrap the uncompressed fetal cranium. The **Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit maneuver** promotes head flexion using the index and middle fingers placed over the fetal maxilla while the other hand exerts gentle occipital traction. Alternatively, specialized Piper forceps or the Burns-Marshall technique safely delivers the aftercoming head.
steps.say: Delivering the head is the most critical stage. The Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit maneuver flexes the head using fingers over the fetal maxilla while traction is applied. Specialized Piper forceps or the Burns-Marshall technique also deliver the head safely.

rows: Jaw flexion and suboccipital downward traction
Grasp ankles, swing body in arc over maternal abdomen
Specialized pelvic curved blades applied beneath body
